what_it_did.what_the_split_means: A mechanical commit republishes an unchanged net -- the report, the dashboard, the state files. Counting those as work would make a quiet day look busy, so they are separated rather than filtered: they happened, they are just not progress.

what_it_decided.thesis_read: Three hours, nine commits, seven substantive, and not one of the three focus items moved. That reads like the fifth stall in a row and it is not one, so the first job of this orientation is to say what actually happened: at 05:39Z the director's console reported "33 newly failing tests at HEAD since 03:16Z", and the machine spent the whole stretch on it. It closed 28 of 28 in `tests/tools`, built the responder-side secret redaction he asked for in the same message (`background/inbound_secret_redaction.py`, wired at nine call sites in `ntfy_responder.py` with the redaction made VISIBLE in the ack rather than silent), and answered his third-time-this-week complaint about waiters with `tools/wait_for.py` and R18 in CLAUDE.md. All three of his console asks landed inside three hours. The work was also good rather than merely fast: the 2022 bill-shock red was closed as a fidelity RESULT with three independent denominators agreeing and an explicit refusal to re-normalise a third time until it passed, and the gas-leg inversion was self-corrected within an hour of its own first finding ("it is heat pumps, not the drawn AQ", then "the inversion was the SPLIT, not either side of it"). A stretch that displaces the direction to answer the director is the direction working, not failing. What did NOT happen is the direction's own spine, and on EP1 I now think every instruction it has been given -- five of them, mine by inheritance -- has been aimed at the wrong thing, including my predecessor's correction of the first four. The story so far was "the hazard is thin, widen its inputs", then "the hazard is borrowed from `saas/churn_model.build_churn_risk`, change whose it is". I verified the second chain and it holds: `simulation/customer_events.py:152` does import `build_churn_risk` and it does feed the world's realised churn through `build_home_move_win_rates`. But it is not the explanation, because the estimator is not thin. The ledger's own `hazard_calibration` publishes THIRTEEN distinct believed hazards over 622 renewal decisions -- 0.05, 0.08, 0.11 ... 0.41, exactly `BASE_ANNUAL_CHURN_PROBABILITY + k x CHURN_UPLIFT_PER_BILL_SHOCK` for k = 0..12 -- with a mean of 0.183 and only 263 of the 622 decisions sitting at the base. The same run's `lifetime_level` recovers a hazard of 0.05 for ALL 33 graded accounts, across nine distinct belief years (11 in 2021, spread 2016 to 2024). If the graded set were any ordinary draw from those decisions, 42% of them would be at the base and 100% of them would not; the probability of thirty-three independent draws all landing there is about one in a trillion. So `distinct_hazards: 1` is not a thin belief and not survivorship. It is a COLLAPSE between two readings of the same company function inside the same run, and nobody has ever localised it -- five instructions in a row proposed a fix without measuring which of the two readings is wrong. There is a named candidate sitting in plain sight: `clv_three_horizon.py:580` takes `hazard = latest.churn_probability` under a time model the code itself calls `LATEST_RENEWAL_CONDITIONED`, one point out of a trajectory of up to thirteen, and the most recent renewal is the one least likely to carry a trailing-twelve-month bill shock. That is a hypothesis and this orientation does not assert it; what it asserts is that the measurement distinguishing it from the alternative takes minutes and has never been run. Against the thesis the headline is unchanged and I will not soften it: the coupled gap is still 2.529, the ledger still stamped 2026-08-26T11:46:22Z, and the company's per-customer CLV still carries less information about realised lifetime margin than assigning every account the population mean. "Decisions customer-by-customer on lifetime value" and a believed tenure of 20.0 years for every graded account remain the same claim and its refutation. But the diagnosis has moved from "the company's belief is thin" to "the company holds a dispersed belief and EP1 reads one number out of it", and those call for opposite work. My predecessor re-armed a trip -- if EP1 does not move on the fifth instruction, decompose it. It did not move. I am discharging that trip rather than overturning it: item one IS the decomposition, cut down from "fix the hazard" to "find which of two readings is wrong", which is the smallest closed-loop test R4 asks for and the first EP1 instruction that can be finished inside one tick. Two other readings. `run_value_cycle_ab` has now gone unrun for five stretches while being named first twice, and after two claim-and-drops the escape hatch my predecessor wrote did not help either -- so the thing nobody has measured is the instruction's own COST. The 2019 ladder ran to completion in a single tick at 04:45; the full-window ask is the same tool over ten years. The nearest working analogue exists and the diff is the window, which makes this an R4 sizing question and not a discipline question, and I have written it that way. And the director's 33 does not reconcile with the machine's 28: the sweep counted `tests/tools`, his report was tree-wide at HEAD, and five reds are unaccounted for by arithmetic alone. That is his number, it is small, and nobody has closed it.

focus.what: Sixth naming, and a SMALLER act than any of the five before it: do not fix the hazard, LOCALISE the collapse, and stop when you know where it is. The measurement is one script and it cannot fail to produce a finding. Take the 33 account ids in `coupled_gap_ledger.json -> EP1_clv_three_horizon.components.lifetime_level.per_account`. For each, rebuild the company's own `churn_risk` map the way `customer_value_view.py:141` does (`build_churn_risk(settlement_records, customers)`) and print, side by side: every `churn_probability` in that account's renewal trajectory, the trajectory length, the value at `[-1]` (which is what `AccountObservables.latest_renewal` returns), and the 0.05 the ledger recovered. Then branch, and say WHICH branch you are in before doing anything else. (a) If the trajectory's last point really is 0.05 for all 33 while earlier points vary, the collapse is the TIME MODEL: `clv_three_horizon.py:580`'s `LATEST_RENEWAL_CONDITIONED` reads one renewal out of up to thirteen and the dispersion is thrown away one line before it is used -- the act is to give H2 a term formed from the trajectory the company already holds (its own mean or trailing-window hazard, your call, argued in the commit message), leaving H1 and H3 alone. (b) If the trajectory DOES vary at `[-1]` and the ledger still recovers 0.05, then the collapse is downstream -- in `build_three_horizon_clv_snapshots`, in the published H1/H2 pair, or in `tools/clv_gap_selection.recover_hazard`'s inversion -- and the act is to fix the instrument, not the company, because then the ledger has been reporting a belief the company does not hold and every EP1 reading for five stretches has been wrong about its own subject. Either way publish the per-account table as a finding under `docs/staging/` before touching any code, so the next reader inherits the measurement even if the fix does not land. Re-measure with `python3 -m tools.couple_clv` and bind the paths with `delivery_lane.record_landing` as each piece lands.
focus.why: This is the thesis's centre and it has resisted five instructions, all of which proposed a cure without a diagnosis. The evidence now says the premise under all five was false: the company's churn estimator produces 13 distinct hazards over 622 decisions (mean 0.183, only 263 at the base), and EP1 recovers 0.05 for all 33 graded accounts across nine belief years. Thirty-three independent draws from that distribution all landing on the base is a one-in-a-trillion event, so this is a mechanism and not a population accident, and it is localisable in minutes. Branch (b) matters as much as (a): if it fires, the harness has been grading a belief the company never formed, which is a tautology-class instrument defect under R15 and a bigger finding than the gap. Finished when the per-account table exists as a named artefact and the document says which branch is true with the evidence attached. Moving the gap is NOT required for this item to be finished, and moving it in the wrong direction does not make the item unfinished -- R12, the gap is a diagnostic. What IS required is that nobody has to ask again where the collapse is. If a changed estimator then puts more than one distinct hazard into the graded population and the coupled rung is genuinely met, a level move is available on that evidence: self-certify with `record_level_up_self_certified`, never `--no-verify` a `level_current` change.

focus.what: Before running anything, MEASURE what the full-window run costs and write the number down. Time one `run_phase4c` pass at full window (or read a wall-clock from the last such run in `docs/observability/`) and compare it against what a worker tick can hold. Then act on what you find, and record which case you were in. If it fits: run `python3 -m tools.run_value_cycle_ab` with no `--end-year`, land it, then run `python3 -m tools.run_price_ladder` with no `--end-year` (or `--rungs 0,0.5,1,2` at FULL window -- keep rung zero, it is the null control the whole reading rests on), and land that. If it does NOT fit, that is the deliverable and it is a better one: file the measured duration as a finding, say plainly that the full-window instrument is not runnable inside the tick that keeps being asked to run it, and name the cheapest thing that would make it runnable (checkpointing, a resumable pass, a longer-lived lane). Either way, edit the headline table in `docs/design/THE_VALUE_CYCLE_REALISED_AB.md` so the current row names the book it ran on -- account count, segment split, git commit -- keeping superseded rows with their supersession notes.
